# Code review {#code-review}

::: {.tada-key}
**Code review** is the process of checking and evaluating each other's code,
either **formally**, as part of the peer-review process, or **informally**, as
co-authors or colleagues. It is critical in avoiding **conceptual, programmatic
and syntactic errors**, and it can take place at any stage of the research cycle.
:::

This chapter follows [Ivimey-Cook et al. (2023)]{.tada-cite key="ivimey-cook-2023"}, *Implementing code review in the
scientific workflow: Insights from ecology and evolutionary biology* (Journal of
Evolutionary Biology 36: 1347–1356, <https://doi.org/10.1111/jeb.14230>).

## Why it is missing, and why it matters {#review-why}

You are probably already using open-source software such as R or Python to
clean, manipulate, visualise and analyse your data. Code-based software is more
transparent and reproducible than point-and-click software, and far more
flexible, since analyses can be tailored to exactly what a study needs.

That flexibility comes at a cost. **Code is more error-prone**
([Budd et al. 1998]{.tada-cite key="budd-1998"}), and several high-profile
retractions have centred on exactly this kind of mistake
([Bolnick & Paull 2009]{.tada-cite key="bolnick-2009"};
[Huijgen et al. 2012]{.tada-cite key="huijgen-2012"};
[Ma & Chang 2007]{.tada-cite key="ma-2007"};
[Miller 2006]{.tada-cite key="miller-2006"};
[Williams & Bürkner 2020]{.tada-cite key="williams-2020"}).

In computer science and software development, code review is routine. In the
academic disciplines that rely on code to make inferences and predictions, it is
**noticeably absent** from the research and publication process
([Indriasari et al. 2020]{.tada-cite key="indriasari-2020"}). Ivimey-Cook et
al. argue for a fundamental shift in research culture that brings code review
into **all stages** of the research process.

There is a structural reason it does not happen. Informal training, combined
with insufficient time and incentives
([Touchon & McCoy 2016]{.tada-cite key="touchon-2016"}), means that coding and
analysis are usually the responsibility of **a single member of a team** for a
project's entire lifetime, in stark contrast to the team-wide collaboration that is normal
when developing methodology and experimental design. That individual character
of research code is precisely what makes pre-publication code review both
unlikely and critical.

## The four Rs {#review-four-rs}

Whatever the stage, the core priorities are the same. The paper frames them as
four questions.

::: {.tada-cards}
::: {.tada-card .t}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reported]{.tada-word}
[Does the code match the description of what is reported in the methods
section?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a1}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Run]{.tada-word}
[Can the code actually be executed?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .d}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reliable]{.tada-word}
[Does the code produce the correct result, and not merely a result, on every
run?]{.tada-gloss}
:::

::: {.tada-card .a2}
[R]{.tada-letter} [Reproducible]{.tada-word}
[Do the outputs match the results reported in the paper?]{.tada-gloss}
:::
:::

::: {.tabset}

### Reported {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code is a key research output and a critical component of scientific
methodology. Open code accompanying written methods sections is becoming more
common, following the same push that produced Open and FAIR data. The first
check is therefore **consistency between the code and the manuscript**, and
these questions catch **conceptual** errors.

*Does the code match what the methods section says was done?* If the methods
state a generalised linear model with Poisson error and the code fits a Gaussian
one, that mismatch has to be part of the review.

**Software and package versions.** At minimum, the packages integral to the
analysis or to visualisation should be listed, with version numbers, somewhere
in the manuscript. In R these can be obtained with `citation()`; in Python,
using `setuptools`. A full list of everything used, including packages involved
in cleaning and tidying, can go elsewhere, such as an associated `.R` or `.py`
file.

This matters beyond bookkeeping. If a package version is later found to contain
a bug, papers depending on it can be identified.

**Environment management** helps here. Packages such as **`renv`**
([Ushey & Wickham 2023]{.tada-cite key="ushey-2023"}), which replaces `packrat` ([Ushey et al. 2022]{.tada-cite key="ushey-2022"}), and
**`groundhog`** ([Simonsohn & Gruson 2023]{.tada-cite key="simonsohn-2023"}) in R, or **`poetry`** ([Eustace 2023]{.tada-cite key="eustace-2023"})
and **`pipenv`** ([Pipenv Maintainer Team 2023]{.tada-cite key="pipenv-2023"}) in Python, help ensure a
reproducible environment and allow specific package versions to be loaded.
Containerisation with **Docker** ([Boettiger 2015]{.tada-cite key="boettiger-2015"}) is another option.

### Run {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Even if code matches the methodology reported in a paper, that does not mean it
is executable. **Programmatic and syntactic errors** can stop code re-running.

Common causes, the first two from the code review paper and the remainder from
the SORTEE guidelines' Stage 5, which lists the same failures from the data
editor's side:

- calls to libraries or modules that are not installed in the current
  environment
- spelling mistakes
- local or absolute file paths that do not exist on the reviewer's machine
- missing files, or filenames in the code that do not match the archived files
- variable names in the code that do not match those in the data files
- a missing code chunk

It is the least demanding of the four checks and the one that fails most often:
74% of over 9,000 archived R files failed to complete without error ([Trisovic
et al. 2022]{.tada-cite key="trisovic-2022"}).

::: {.tada-tip}
Run it in a **fresh session**, from a **fresh download**, in a **new folder**.
Anything that only works because of what is already loaded in your environment
will fail here, which is what the check is for.
:::

### Reliable {.unlisted .unnumbered}

This is the hardest of the four checks, and the one that most needs a reviewer
who knows the study.

Errors can propagate through code that runs perfectly well and produces an
output, because **code can produce incorrect results in a reproducible manner**,
returning the same wrong answer every time. The paper's example: if code selects
or modifies the wrong column in a dataset, the analysis is wrong but nothing
errors.

**Unit testing** helps, through **`testthat`** ([Wickham 2011]{.tada-cite key="wickham-2011"}) in R and
**`pytest`** ([Okken 2022]{.tada-cite key="okken-2022"}) in Python. But this type of error remains common and
is **extremely difficult to pick up by anyone without deep familiarity with the
dataset and code**. It is also thought to scale with the number of lines and the
complexity of the code ([Lipow 1982]{.tada-cite key="lipow-1982"}).

::: {.tada-note}
This is the strongest argument for **co-author** review over external review. A
reviewer who does not know your data cannot tell that `mass` should have been
`mass_g`. A co-author can.
:::

### Reproducible {.unlisted .unnumbered}

The most fundamental question is whether **the code can produce the output, and
thus support the conclusions, given in the paper.**

The final step of code review is ensuring that outputs, when the code is re-run,
match those reported in the analysis and results sections, including relevant
figures and the narrative text within those sections.

**When exact matching is not possible.** Apply some tolerance, especially with
stochastic methods where parameter estimates change between runs, or with
techniques that are computationally demanding and slow. This happens, for
example, when `set.seed()` (R) or `random.seed()` (Python) was not used before
stochastic sampling.

Providing model outputs helps. Save them with `saveRDS()` in R or
`pickle.dump()` in Python, though this does not let a reviewer run the code
themselves to see whether they obtain similar results. Where the code cannot be
re-run in reasonable time, compare the newly generated results against those
originally reported.

The literature offers two criteria for judging a match.

*Conclusion and numbers* ([Archmiller et al. 2020]{.tada-cite key="archmiller-2020"}). Compare the **conclusion**,
meaning direction and significance level, and the **numbers**, meaning intervals
matching within one significant figure. Their worked example:

| Original | Reproduced | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.12, interval 3.45–4.91 | Conclusion **and** numbers reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 6.5, interval 6.0–7.0 | Same conclusion; numbers **not** quantitatively reproduced |
| mean 4.00, interval 3.30–5.00 | mean 4.10, interval −1.00–8.40 | **Not** reproduced, because the interval now overlaps zero |

*Percentage error* ([Hardwicke et al. 2021]{.tada-cite key="hardwicke-2021"}; see also [Kambouris et al. 2024]{.tada-cite key="kambouris-2024"}).
Comparison at one significant figure is highly dependent on scale, whereas
percentage error is not. Using

$$\text{PE} = \frac{\text{new} - \text{original}}{\text{original}} \times 100$$

error is classified as **non-existent** when this value is 0, **minor** between
0 and 10, and **major (and not reproducible)** at 10 or above. Note that the
formula as published is signed; in practice it is the absolute value that is
compared against those thresholds.

As well as the overlap with 0, or with the null hypothesis, not changing, the
reported and reproduced estimates and intervals should not differ significantly
from each other. With stochastic MCMC methods, variation between chains is
expected to be much lower than variation within a chain, so the reproduced value
should sit well within the reported credible interval.

:::

## Writing reviewable code {#review-reviewable}

Good readability is what makes effective code review possible at all. The paper
offers four solutions:

1. **Call packages explicitly** via the namespace: `package::function()` in R,
   `package.module.function()` in Python.
2. **Use relative file paths**, for example the `here` package
   ([Müller & Bryan 2020]{.tada-cite key="muller-bryan-2020"}), preferably with an associated R project file if using
   R and RStudio, or a virtual environment in Python.
3. **Remove redundant packages.**
4. **Write analysis code with clear subheadings, intuitive comments and
   easy-to-understand object names.**

For style tooling, **`styler`** ([Müller & Walthert 2020]{.tada-cite key="muller-walthert-2020"}) reformats R code to a
standard style in one command, while **`pycodestyle`** ([Rocholl 2022]{.tada-cite key="rocholl-2022"}) checks
Python code against PEP 8. Supported styles include Google and tidyverse in R,
and PEP 8 in Python.

Literate formats, meaning R and Python Markdown, Quarto, and Jupyter Notebook or
JupyterLab, present code in chunks which, with suitably descriptive comments,
are far easier to read. See [Annotated](#annotated-literate).

### Structure {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A simple folder and file structure goes a long way towards helping researchers
at all skill levels understand the **order and flow** of an analysis:

- **Sequentially labelled** subfolders and scripts, so that someone following
  the code knows the order to run things in, with files beginning `01…`, `02…`
- **Folders named for their purpose**, such as `data`, `scripts` and `functions`
- **Raw data kept separate**, so that it is not accidentally modified or
  overwritten when cleaning or wrangling code runs
- A **README** and additional metadata giving the signposts needed to re-run the
  code: packages and version numbers, descriptions of the data files, the
  project aim, author contact details, and any licences in place

It is also crucial to **explain what data cleaning or curation happened before
the analysis code**, meaning what previous manipulation or pre-processing
produced the data in its current state, or where an intermediate data file was
used.

::: {.tada-note}
**Metadata tooling.** Packages such as `codemeta` ([Boettiger 2017]{.tada-cite key="boettiger-2017"}) and
`dataReporter` ([Petersen & Ekstrøm 2019]{.tada-cite key="petersen-2019"}) in R, or `CodeMetaPy` ([van Gompel 2023]{.tada-cite key="van-gompel-2023"})
and `cookiecutter` ([Feldroy 2022]{.tada-cite key="feldroy-2022"}) in Python, can help produce consistent
metadata and project templates. Pipeline tools automate the steps from raw
dataset to results: `targets` ([Landau 2021]{.tada-cite key="landau-2021"}) and `workflowr`
([Blischak et al. 2019]{.tada-cite key="blischak-2019"}) in R, and `luigi` ([The Luigi Authors 2023]{.tada-cite key="luigi-authors-2023"}) in Python.
:::

## When code review happens {#review-when}

Code review can begin as early as the first initiation of a project, and it has
a role beyond publication.

::: {.tabset}

### Pre-submission {.unlisted .unnumbered}

**This is where most of the value is.** It is also the stage where a reviewer
can catch *Reliable* errors, because they know the study.

Keep **continuous code collaboration at all stages** of a manuscript.
Collaboration can be facilitated by code-sharing platforms such as GitHub, where
users can submit and comment on pull requests. At SORTEE, GitHub issues were
used to summarise the discussion of an individual's code.

The [SORTEE guidelines](#sortee) make the same recommendation directly to
authors, under "Perform a pre-submission code review"; see
[Advice for authors](#sharing-authors) for what that review should cover.

### During peer review {.unlisted .unnumbered}

This is one of the most crucial places for code review, because reviewers can
follow the logic of the analyses carefully, much as they follow the argument
from introduction to discussion.

Some journals already request code and data at submission, including
[The Royal Society]{.tada-cite key="royal-society-2023"},
*[Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology]{.tada-cite key="bakker-2020"}* and
*[The American Naturalist]{.tada-cite key="bolnick-2022"}*, though the paper's
authors note that in their experience this is not enforced. In some cases, such
as the **Journal of Open Source Software**, the entire formal peer-review
process, code and manuscript alike, is hosted on GitHub.

The benefits run both ways
([Fernández-Juricic 2021]{.tada-cite key="fernandez-juricic-2021"}). For
authors, providing code during peer review could increase manuscript quality.
For reviewers, available code gives far deeper insight, because there is a
clearer link between experimental methodology and statistical analysis, which
is the first R, code **as reported**.

There are two practical obstacles.

*Finding reviewers.* There is already a shortage of willing reviewers. It is
reasonable to expect a reviewer to check that code is **as reported**, but
anything deeper takes time from already overworked academics who may not have
the exact expertise. A workable compromise is for reviewers to state whether
they are competent to check that the code is as reported, and for the journal to
ensure **at least one** reviewer has checked the code.

*Double-blind review.* Anonymised data and code can be submitted directly to the
journal, for example as a zip file, or uploaded to Figshare, OSF, GitHub or
Dryad, which allow authors to provide an **anonymised link** for peer review.

### Post-publication {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Post-publication review is much less discussed. It cannot prevent the
publication of incorrect results, but it does allow the four Rs to be checked
after the fact.

The first question is simply whether **all the code used to produce the results
has been made available**. If it has not, the main option is to contact the
corresponding author, or the journal, and ask, much as data are requested "upon
reasonable request".

**If you find that the code does not adhere to one of the Rs:**

1. **Contact the corresponding author**, or, if the paper uses the MeRIT system,
   the person who actually conducted the analysis. A GitHub issue works well if
   there is a repository; otherwise, email.
2. **Rule out benign causes** first, such as differences in software version, in
   R or in package versions, or inherent stochasticity from simulations and MCMC
   sampling.
3. **Let the authors go to the journal themselves.** If there is a genuine
   error, authors should be given the chance to contact the journal to highlight
   and correct their own mistake.

::: {.tada-note}
Journal culture matters here. Under *The American Naturalist*'s stance
([Bolnick 2022]{.tada-cite key="bolnick-2022"}), authors who contact the journal to correct code or data errors
are **not penalised**, and corrections are encouraged where warranted. Where
updated results would alter the narrative of a published paper, corrections are
harder; publication versioning or "living" documents may be a first step
([Kane & Amin 2023]{.tada-cite key="kane-2023"}).
:::

:::

## Running a code club {#review-club}

A code club is one of the most effective ways to establish peer code review
within a lab or among colleagues. The following draws on the authors' experience
building a code review club in collaboration with **SORTEE**.

The barriers being addressed are worth naming, because the design of the club
follows from them ([Gomes et al. 2022]{.tada-cite key="gomes-2022"}): **lack of time and incentive**, **lack of
technical knowledge and unclear workflows**, and **social pressures and the fear
of being judged by peers**.

### Set a clear goal for each session {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Is the focus **general learning and improving readability**, or is it to
**error-check and scrutinise reproducibility**? A clear structure and goal for
each session focuses comments and advice on the precise reason for the review.

Relatedly, unless the aim is specifically to evaluate different analytical
options, it is better to **leave methodological questions aside**. A session
that drifts into the choice of model is no longer reviewing the code.

### Make it a judgement-free environment {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Volunteers often feel very anxious about showing code that may have errors. It
is vital to **normalise the existence of errors** and to highlight that
perfection is never possible. It is also useful to stress that **there is no
such thing as bad code** ([Barnes 2010]{.tada-cite key="barnes-2010"}), and that there are usually multiple ways
to approach the same problem.

### Think about group size {.unlisted .unnumbered}

A **smaller group** is a friendlier starting point, since people feel more
comfortable speaking up and it better facilitates peer-to-peer learning and
focused review. **Larger groups** work better for wider discussion of general
themes and tips. Choose by aim: larger groups for general discussion, smaller
ones for focused review of a specific script.

### Decide on credit {.unlisted .unnumbered}

Code review outside the formal peer-review process can have a large impact on a
project, from error checking to validating that statistical analyses are
appropriate. So what should reviewers get?

- **Acknowledgement via MeRIT** (Method Reporting with Initials for
  Transparency), for example: *"…mixed model with a Gaussian error distribution.
  Code was checked by E.I.C."*
- **Co-authorship**, where the review fundamentally altered the project and the
  resulting paper, for instance where a reviewer finds a major coding error
  that, once fixed, changes the results and conclusions.

The paper's principle is that incentives should be proportionate to the
reviewer's impact on the project.

## A reviewer's script {#review-script}

Wiki guidance: a practical sequence for a single review session, built on the
four Rs. The full checklist is at
[`templates/code-review-checklist.md`](templates/code-review-checklist.md).

**Before the session (reviewer, 20 minutes)**

1. Download the project into a **new, empty folder**.
2. Open the README. Can you tell what to run, in what order, and what you need
   installed? Note anything you had to guess.
3. Try to run it, in a **fresh session**. Record every error verbatim, and stop
   at the first one you cannot resolve in two minutes.

**In the session**

4. **Reported.** Walk the methods section against the code, section by section.
   Flag anything described in the paper you cannot find in the code, and
   anything in the code not described in the paper.
5. **Run.** Go through the errors you hit. Most will be environment or path
   problems, and most are quick.
6. **Reliable.** Pick the two or three steps where a silent error would matter
   most, such as the filtering step, the join, or the model specification, and
   read them closely with the author. Ask what each column is.
7. **Reproducible.** Take three numbers from the results section and find them
   in the output.

**Afterwards**

8. Write it up as a short list, ordered by severity, separating **must fix**
   from **would be nice**.
9. Agree how the reviewer will be credited.

::: {.tada-tip}
**Give feedback on the code, not the coder.** "This line reads `mass`, is that
the right column?" is easier to act on than "you used the wrong column". Fear of
being judged is one of the three barriers the paper identifies, so how comments
are phrased affects whether people keep volunteering.
:::

## Checklist {#review-checklist}

- [ ] **Reported.** The code does what the methods section says it does
- [ ] Software and key packages, with versions, are stated
- [ ] **Run.** The code executes from a fresh download in a fresh session
- [ ] All required libraries are installed and loaded within the code
- [ ] File paths are relative and resolve
- [ ] **Reliable.** Filtering, joins and model specifications have been read closely by someone who knows the data
- [ ] Seeds are set before stochastic steps
- [ ] **Reproducible.** Spot-checked numbers from the results section match the output
- [ ] Mismatches are explained (version, stochasticity, post-processing) and documented
- [ ] Slow or proprietary steps have saved outputs archived
- [ ] The reviewer's contribution is credited (MeRIT, acknowledgement, or authorship)
